title: Foundational Document on the Manufacturing Service

sections.title: Core Purpose
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service provides the Ben Franklin Society with fabrication and manufacturing capacity—the ability to make, repair, and modify physical things. It is community productive infrastructure of the most fundamental kind. Every other service depends in some degree on the ability to fabricate and maintain the physical objects their functions require.
sections.rationale: Physical things break. Custom parts are needed. A community that can only consume what others manufacture is a community whose resilience depends entirely on systems it does not control.

sections.title: Dual Role
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service operates in two complementary modes. It manufactures and fabricates directly—making parts, components, and products as needed by the community's services, institutions, and members. And it supports—providing equipment access, technical expertise, and workspace to member associations and individuals undertaking their own fabrication work.
sections.rationale: Both modes serve the community's productive capacity. Distributed community capability is more resilient than capacity concentrated only in the Service itself.

sections.title: Scope
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service's scope encompasses the full range of fabrication disciplines—metal forming and welding, machining, woodworking, electronics fabrication and repair, general fabrication, and such other manufacturing disciplines as the community develops capacity for.
sections.rationale: No fabrication need that the community has is outside the Service's scope if the Service can develop the capacity to address it.

sections.title: Resilience Function
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service's deepest value is resilience. A community that can fabricate its own parts is a community that can maintain its infrastructure, repair its equipment, and adapt its physical environment without depending on external supply chains for every component.
sections.rationale: This resilience function informs how the Service is built and operated—prioritizing broad capability over narrow specialization, and community skill development over Service-only expertise.

sections.title: Oversight
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service is overseen by the College of Fabricators, which sets technical standards for fabrication practice, safety, and quality, and credentials manufacturing practitioners.
sections.rationale: The College's broad technical knowledge base makes it the natural home for manufacturing oversight across the full range of fabrication disciplines.

sections.title: Metal Fabrication
sections.body: Metal fabrication—cutting, forming, welding, and finishing metal components—is the Manufacturing Service's primary and most critical capability. Metal parts are required by virtually every other community service and by agricultural, household, and infrastructure maintenance throughout the community.
sections.rationale: The Service shall develop and maintain comprehensive metal fabrication capability including welding, cutting, forming, and finishing across common metals.

sections.title: Machining
sections.body: Machining—the precise shaping of metal and other materials through cutting, turning, milling, and drilling—enables the production of custom parts to exact specifications. Machining capability transforms the Manufacturing Service from a general fabrication shop into a genuine precision manufacturing resource.
sections.rationale: The Service shall develop and maintain machining capability including lathe, mill, and drill press operations.

sections.title: Woodworking
sections.body: Woodworking capability supports construction, furniture, agricultural implements, and such other community needs as require wood fabrication. The community's agricultural and housing functions in particular generate ongoing woodworking needs.
sections.rationale: The Service shall maintain woodworking capability appropriate to the community's needs.

sections.title: Electronics
sections.body: Electronics fabrication and repair capability enables the community to maintain, repair, and in some cases manufacture the electronic components that its energy systems, communication systems, and equipment depend upon.
sections.rationale: As electronic devices become increasingly central to community infrastructure, the ability to repair rather than replace them becomes increasingly important.

sections.title: Capability Development
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service shall continuously develop its capabilities—acquiring new equipment, training practitioners in new disciplines, and expanding the range of what the community can make.
sections.rationale: The College of Fabricators shall guide capability development toward the areas of greatest community need.

sections.title: Material Acquisition
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service shall attain raw materials from wherever they can be found—recovered metals from the Sanitation Service's material recovery function, purchased stock when available and affordable, salvaged materials from decommissioned equipment and structures, inter-society trade, and such other sources as the community can access.
sections.rationale: Material acquisition is a standing operational function, not a one-time procurement exercise.

sections.title: Sanitation Service Coordination
sections.body: Recovered metals from the Sanitation Service's material recovery function are a primary raw material source for the Manufacturing Service. The two services shall maintain formal coordination protocols—the Sanitation Service communicating what metals are available and in what condition, the Manufacturing Service communicating what materials it needs.
sections.rationale: Waste metal flowing into productive fabrication is the community material loop operating as intended.

sections.title: Strategic Reserves
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service shall maintain strategic reserves of the most critical raw materials—particularly common metals and fasteners that are required across a wide range of fabrication work.
sections.rationale: Reserves buffer the Service against supply disruptions and ensure that urgent fabrication needs can be met even when procurement is difficult.

sections.title: Inter-Society Trade
sections.body: Raw materials may be traded between Ben Franklin Societies through the federation's commerce infrastructure. A society with surplus metal stock and a society needing it can exchange through the clearinghouse.
sections.rationale: The Manufacturing Service shall participate in inter-society material trade as both a supplier and a recipient.

sections.title: Community Services Priority
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service shall prioritize fabrication work for the community's other services—the Energy Service needing custom mounting hardware, the Agricultural Service needing equipment repair, the Housing Service needing fabricated components, the Health Service needing instrument repair, the Fire and Emergency Service needing vehicle parts.
sections.rationale: Community service needs are the Manufacturing Service's primary production mandate.

sections.title: Energy Service
sections.body: Solar panel mounting, battery enclosures, electrical conduit fabrication, and such other energy infrastructure components as require custom fabrication shall be a standing Manufacturing Service function.
sections.rationale: The Energy Service and Manufacturing Service shall coordinate on infrastructure development to ensure fabrication capacity is available when installation requires it.

sections.title: Agricultural Service
sections.body: Farm equipment repair and fabrication is among the most practically important Manufacturing Service functions. When a tractor breaks at planting time or a grain mill needs a replacement part, the Manufacturing Service is the community's recourse.
sections.rationale: The Service shall develop and maintain agricultural equipment repair capability as a priority function.

sections.title: Member Access
sections.body: Beyond community services the Manufacturing Service supports member associations and individual members in their own fabrication work. Members with farming operations, construction projects, equipment maintenance needs, or creative fabrication work may access the Service's equipment, workspace, and expertise.
sections.rationale: Community productive capacity distributed across members who can use it is more resilient than capacity concentrated only in the Service itself.

sections.title: Production for Community Needs
sections.body: Where the community's needs justify production runs—standard fasteners, common fittings, replacement parts for community equipment—the Manufacturing Service shall produce them.
sections.rationale: Community-manufactured standard components reduce dependence on external supply chains for the most commonly needed parts.

sections.title: Community Equipment
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service's equipment—lathes, mills, welders, drill presses, saws, and such other fabrication tools as the Service maintains—is community property held in trust for community productive use. Equipment shall be maintained in safe working order, made available for community and member use according to established protocols, and replaced or expanded as community needs and resources allow.
sections.rationale: Well-maintained equipment produces quality work and operates safely. Poor maintenance creates hazards and poor results.

sections.title: Safety Standards
sections.body: Manufacturing equipment is inherently hazardous. The Manufacturing Service shall maintain rigorous safety standards—personal protective equipment requirements, equipment guarding, ventilation for welding and finishing operations, fire prevention, and such other safety measures as the work requires. Safety training shall be required before any member accesses manufacturing equipment.
sections.rationale: The College of Fabricators shall establish and enforce safety standards.

sections.title: Workspace
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service shall maintain workspace adequate to its fabrication functions—sufficient floor space for equipment and work in progress, appropriate lighting, ventilation, and utilities, and organized storage for materials and finished work.
sections.rationale: Workspace is as important as equipment. A cluttered, inadequate workspace produces unsafe and poor quality work.

sections.title: Knowledge as Infrastructure
sections.body: Manufacturing knowledge—how to weld, how to operate a lathe, how to read technical drawings, how to select materials, how to troubleshoot fabrication problems—is as important as the equipment itself. A shop full of equipment without people who know how to use it is not a manufacturing service.
sections.rationale: The Manufacturing Service shall treat knowledge development and transmission as a core function equal in importance to production.

sections.title: Practitioner Credentialing
sections.body: The College of Fabricators shall credential Manufacturing Service practitioners—assessing competence in specific fabrication disciplines and authorizing practice at appropriate levels.
sections.rationale: Credentialing ensures that the people operating manufacturing equipment are genuinely competent to do so safely and productively.

sections.title: Member Training
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service shall actively train community members in fabrication skills—welding, basic machining, woodworking, electronics repair, and such other skills as the community needs distributed broadly. Training programs shall be accessible to members regardless of prior experience.
sections.rationale: The goal is a community in which fabrication knowledge is held widely, not concentrated only in the Manufacturing Service's staff.

sections.title: Apprenticeship
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service shall maintain an apprenticeship model for developing skilled fabricators—pairing less experienced members with experienced practitioners for hands-on learning in specific disciplines.
sections.rationale: Apprenticeship transmits the tacit knowledge that formal training alone cannot capture: how a cut feels when it is right, how a weld sounds when it is good, how a material behaves under specific conditions.

sections.title: Annual Report
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service shall publish an annual report covering: fabrication work completed by discipline and volume; community services supported and work performed; member and association access utilization; raw materials acquired by source; equipment inventory and condition; training programs and participation; apprenticeship activity; inter-society coordination; and any significant developments in manufacturing capacity.
sections.rationale: The report shall be presented to the General Assembly and made available to all members.

sections.title: Capability Transparency
sections.body: The Manufacturing Service shall communicate clearly to the community what fabrication capabilities it currently has, what it cannot yet do, and what it is working toward.
sections.rationale: Community services and members planning projects need honest information about what the Manufacturing Service can deliver and when.

sections.title: Material Inventory
sections.body: Current raw material inventory shall be reported to the Assembly quarterly and made available to community services and members planning fabrication work.
sections.rationale: Services and members who know what materials are available can plan their fabrication work accordingly.
